---
title: "Use cases: three applied questions"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4,
  dpi = 150
)
library(regsensitivity)
library(ggplot2)

# Percent with no decimals, for breakdown points stored as fractions.
pct <- function(x) formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = 0)
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
```

Each of the three studies below asks a causal question with a
regression, and each has an omitted variable that a referee would raise.
They come from labour economics, the economics of discrimination, and the
economics of education. All three data sets ship with the
[AER](https://cran.r-project.org/package=AER) package, so every number
here can be reproduced.

Each study follows the same recipe:

1. Write the regression and choose the **calibration covariates**
   (`compare`): the observed variables whose relation to the treatment
   is a yardstick for the omitted one.
2. Compute the **breakdown point** for the sign of the coefficient. This
   is how strong selection on unobservables has to be, relative to
   selection on the calibration covariates, before the sign can flip.
   Compute it for exogenous controls (`cbar = 0`) and for arbitrarily
   endogenous ones (`cbar = 1`).
3. Read it against the **reference values** from `calibrate_rho()`, the
   same ratio computed for each calibration covariate in turn.
4. Report Oster's $\delta$ next to it, and say which assumption each
   number rests on.

The three studies end with three different verdicts, and the point is how
the numbers produce them. [Interpreting results](../articles/interpreting-results.html)
explains each quantity in detail on simulated data, where the truth is
known.

## 1. Returns to schooling

How much does a year of schooling raise wages? The classic worry is
ability: people who stay in school longer may also earn more for reasons
that have nothing to do with schooling. Ability is not in the data.

The `CPS1985` data (Berndt 1991) has 534 workers from the 1985 Current
Population Survey. We regress log wages on years of education, with
experience and demographic controls. Occupation and sector are left out
on purpose, because they are partly outcomes of schooling; controlling for
them would absorb part of the effect we want to measure.

```{r wage-data}
data("CPS1985", package = "AER")
CPS1985$lwage <- log(CPS1985$wage)

f_wage <- lwage ~ education + experience + I(experience^2) +
  gender + ethnicity + union + married + region
w_wage <- c("experience", "gender", "ethnicity", "union", "married")
```

The calibration covariates are the controls that plausibly share
ability's relation to schooling: experience, gender, ethnicity, union
status and marital status. Region stays as a control but not as a yardstick.

```{r wage}
wage_bk <- regsen_breakdown(f_wage, CPS1985, compare = w_wage,
                            cbar = seq(0, 1, 0.1))
wage_bnd <- regsen_bounds(f_wage, CPS1985, compare = w_wage, cbar = 1)
wage_rho <- calibrate_rho(f_wage, CPS1985, compare = w_wage)

wage_bp <- as.data.frame(wage_bk)
coef(wage_bnd)
wage_bp[wage_bp$index %in% c(0, 0.5, 1), ]
wage_rho
```

```{r wage-numbers, include = FALSE}
wage_b   <- coef(wage_bnd)[["medium"]]
wage_bp0 <- wage_bp$breakdown[wage_bp$index == 0]
wage_bp1 <- wage_bp$breakdown[wage_bp$index == 1]
wage_top <- wage_rho[which.max(wage_rho$rho), ]
wage_2nd <- sort(wage_rho$rho, decreasing = TRUE)[2]
n_hisp   <- sum(CPS1985$ethnicity == "hispanic")
```

A year of schooling is associated with wages about
`r fmt(100 * wage_b, 1)`% higher (the coefficient is in log points). With
exogenous controls, the positive sign survives until selection on
unobservables is `r pct(wage_bp0)`% as strong as selection on the five
calibration covariates together. With endogenous controls the threshold
falls to `r pct(wage_bp1)`%.

The reference values set the scale. No calibration covariate exceeds
`r fmt(wage_2nd, 0)`% except the Hispanic indicator, at
`r fmt(wage_top$rho, 0)`%, which describes `r n_hisp` of the 534 workers.
So even with endogenous controls, the omitted variable would have to
predict schooling roughly as well as all the calibration covariates
combined: far better than experience, gender, union status or marital
status, and about as well as ethnicity does in this sample.

That is a precise statement of the debate rather than an end to it.
Someone who believes ability predicts schooling more strongly than
experience, gender, ethnicity, union status and marital status do together
has a case that the sign is not identified. Someone who doubts it does
not. The number tells both sides where the line is.

## 2. Race and mortgage denials

Do lenders deny mortgages to Black applicants more often than to white
applicants with the same credit profile? The `HMDA` data, from the Boston
Fed study of Munnell et al. (1996), has 2,380 applications with the
credit variables the lender saw. The worry is that lenders also saw
things the data do not record, and that these are related to race.

The outcome is a denial indicator, so this is a linear probability model.
The calibration covariates are the credit variables, because the
unrecorded information is more of the same kind: payment-to-income and
housing-expense ratios, the loan-to-value ratio, consumer and mortgage
credit history, public bad-credit records, and whether mortgage insurance
was denied.

```{r hmda-data}
data("HMDA", package = "AER")
HMDA$deny01 <- as.numeric(HMDA$deny == "yes")

f_hmda <- deny01 ~ afam + pirat + hirat + lvrat + chist + mhist + phist +
  insurance + selfemp + single + hschool + unemp + condomin
w_hmda <- c("pirat", "hirat", "lvrat", "chist", "mhist", "phist",
            "insurance")
```

```{r hmda}
hmda_bk <- regsen_breakdown(f_hmda, HMDA, compare = w_hmda,
                            cbar = seq(0, 1, 0.1))
hmda_bnd <- regsen_bounds(f_hmda, HMDA, compare = w_hmda, cbar = 1)
hmda_rho <- calibrate_rho(f_hmda, HMDA, compare = w_hmda)

hmda_bp <- as.data.frame(hmda_bk)
coef(hmda_bnd)
hmda_bp[hmda_bp$index %in% c(0, 0.5, 1), ]
head(hmda_rho, 4)
```

```{r hmda-numbers, include = FALSE}
hmda_short <- coef(hmda_bnd)[["short"]]
hmda_b     <- coef(hmda_bnd)[["medium"]]
hmda_bp0   <- hmda_bp$breakdown[hmda_bp$index == 0]
hmda_bp1   <- hmda_bp$breakdown[hmda_bp$index == 1]
```

Without controls, Black applicants are denied
`r fmt(100 * hmda_short, 1)` percentage points more often. The credit
variables cut the gap to `r fmt(100 * hmda_b, 1)` points, so observed
credit differences already explain more than half of it. That is exactly
the pattern that makes a remaining gap fragile: if the observed credit
variables matter this much, the unobserved ones may as well.

The breakdown point puts a number on it. An omitted variable whose
relation to race is only `r pct(hmda_bp1)`% as strong as that of the
observed credit variables together is enough to remove the gap. Allowing
the controls to be endogenous barely matters here (`r pct(hmda_bp0)`% with
exogenous controls). Several single credit variables have reference
values above that threshold; the worst consumer-credit category
(`chist6`) alone is at `r fmt(hmda_rho$rho[1], 0)`%. One more credit
variable of that kind, left out of the data, could account for the whole
gap.

### The same data through Oster's $\delta$

The conventional robustness check reads differently.

```{r hmda-oster}
r2rel <- c(1.3, 1.6, 2)
hmda_osc <- regsen_breakdown(f_hmda, HMDA, compare = w_hmda,
                             analysis = "oster",
                             r2long = r2rel, r2long_type = "relative")
hmda_oea <- regsen_breakdown(f_hmda, HMDA, compare = w_hmda,
                             analysis = "oster",
                             r2long = 1.3, r2long_type = "relative",
                             beta = bnd_eq(0))
data.frame(r2long = paste0(r2rel, " x R2"),
           sign_change = as.data.frame(hmda_osc)$breakdown)
breakdown_point(hmda_oea, signed = TRUE)
```

```{r hmda-oster-numbers, include = FALSE}
hmda_ea  <- breakdown_point(hmda_oea, signed = TRUE)
hmda_sc2 <- as.data.frame(hmda_osc)$breakdown[3]
```

At Oster's rule of thumb, $R_{\max} = 1.3 R^2$, the explain-away $\delta$
is `r fmt(hmda_ea, 2)`, and the sign change point is capped at one: by the
usual $|\delta| \geq 1$ convention, the gap is robust. Setting
$R_{\max}$ to twice $R^2$ instead brings the sign change point down to
`r fmt(hmda_sc2, 2)`.

The two analyses rest on different assumptions. Oster's comfortable
number depends on $R_{\max}$, which limits how much of the outcome the
omitted variable can explain. The DMP breakdown point above leaves that
unrestricted (`rybar = Inf`) and does not assume the controls are
exogenous. A write-up should report both, and say which assumption
carries the conclusion. Here it is the cap on $R_{\max}$.

## 3. Class size and test scores

Do smaller classes raise test scores? The `CASchools` data (Stock and
Watson) has 420 California school districts. The worry is that districts
with small classes differ in ways that also raise scores, such as wealth or
parental involvement. This is the second application in the package's
R Journal article.

The average reading and mathematics score is regressed on the
student-teacher ratio, with county fixed effects as controls. The
English-learner share and the free-lunch share serve as calibration
covariates, because they are proxies for the same disadvantage that the
omitted variables would capture.

```{r school-data}
data("CASchools", package = "AER")
CASchools$score <- with(CASchools, (read + math) / 2)
CASchools$STR   <- with(CASchools, students / teachers)

f_sch <- score ~ STR + english + lunch + county
w_sch <- c("english", "lunch")
```

```{r school}
sch_bk  <- regsen_breakdown(f_sch, CASchools, compare = w_sch,
                            cbar = seq(0, 1, 0.1))
sch_bnd <- regsen_bounds(f_sch, CASchools, compare = w_sch, cbar = 1)
sch_rho <- calibrate_rho(f_sch, CASchools, compare = w_sch)

sch_bp <- as.data.frame(sch_bk)
coef(sch_bnd)
sch_bp[sch_bp$index %in% c(0, 0.5, 1), ]
sch_rho
```

```{r school-numbers, include = FALSE}
sch_b   <- coef(sch_bnd)[["medium"]]
sch_bp0 <- sch_bp$breakdown[sch_bp$index == 0]
sch_bp1 <- sch_bp$breakdown[sch_bp$index == 1]
```

One more student per teacher is associated with a
`r fmt(abs(sch_b), 2)`-point lower score. Here the assumption about the
controls is decisive. With exogenous controls the negative sign survives
until selection on unobservables is `r pct(sch_bp0)`% as strong as
selection on the two calibration covariates, far above either reference
value. Once the controls are allowed to be endogenous, the threshold falls
to `r pct(sch_bp1)`%, between the English-learner share
(`r fmt(sch_rho$rho[sch_rho$variable == "english"], 0)`%) and the
free-lunch share (`r fmt(sch_rho$rho[sch_rho$variable == "lunch"], 0)`%).

So whether the conclusion is robust depends on a question the regression
cannot answer: are the controls themselves correlated with the omitted
variables? If county effects and the two shares are clean, the finding is
robust. If they are not, an omitted variable no more important for class
size than the free-lunch share could reverse the sign.

## The three side by side

```{r compare-plot, fig.alt = "Breakdown point against cbar for the three studies. The class-size and schooling curves almost coincide: they start near 2.9 and 2.75 at cbar = 0 and fall to about 0.94 at cbar = 1, crossing a dashed line at one near cbar = 0.8. The mortgage curve is flat at about 0.31 throughout."}
both <- rbind(
  data.frame(study = "Returns to schooling", wage_bp),
  data.frame(study = "Race and mortgage denials", hmda_bp),
  data.frame(study = "Class size and test scores", sch_bp)
)
ggplot(both, aes(index, breakdown, colour = study)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_regsen() +
  labs(x = "cbar (how endogenous the controls may be)",
       y = "Breakdown point for the sign (rxbar)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_regsen(legend_position = "bottom")
```

The dashed line is a breakdown point of one: selection on unobservables as
strong as selection on all calibration covariates together. It is a
benchmark, not a cutoff.

The schooling and class-size curves almost coincide, yet the two studies
do not reach the same verdict. A breakdown point is a ratio against the
calibration covariates, and those differ. In the wage study, only an
indicator for `r n_hisp` workers predicts schooling as strongly as the
threshold requires. In the class-size study, the free-lunch share, the
main observed proxy for disadvantage, already exceeds it. The verdict
comes from comparing the breakdown point with the reference values and
with what you know about the omitted variable.

| Study | Coefficient | Breakdown, exogenous controls | Breakdown, endogenous controls | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Returns to schooling | `r fmt(100 * wage_b, 1)`% per year | `r pct(wage_bp0)`% | `r pct(wage_bp1)`% | Holds unless ability predicts schooling about as well as all calibration covariates combined |
| Race and mortgage denials | `r fmt(100 * hmda_b, 1)` points | `r pct(hmda_bp0)`% | `r pct(hmda_bp1)`% | Fragile: one more credit variable of the observed kind could explain the gap |
| Class size and test scores | `r fmt(sch_b, 2)` points per student | `r pct(sch_bp0)`% | `r pct(sch_bp1)`% | Holds with exogenous controls; with endogenous ones, an omitted variable like the free-lunch share could reverse it |

## Adapting the recipe to your data

* **Choose `compare` before you look at the numbers.** The breakdown point
  is relative to the calibration covariates, so this choice is the main
  substantive decision in the analysis. Pick variables whose relation to
  the treatment is a fair analogue of the omitted variable's.
* **Leave out bad controls.** Variables caused by the treatment, such as
  occupation in the wage regression, change what the coefficient means.
  The sensitivity analysis cannot fix that.
* **Report the whole curve in `cbar`,** or at least both ends. As the
  class-size study shows, the answer can hinge on it.
* **Report Oster's $\delta$ with its $R_{\max}$,** and the sign change
  value rather than only the explain-away one. As the mortgage study
  shows, the two frameworks can disagree, and the reason is an assumption
  you can name.
* **Add a confidence interval** for the breakdown point with
  `regsen_boot()` before publishing (see
  [Interpreting results, Case 9](../articles/interpreting-results.html)).
* **Format the result for the paper** with `regsen_table()` or
  `modelsummary` (see [Plots and tables](../articles/plots-and-tables.html)).

Used the package on your own data? A short
[usage report](https://github.com/mikenguyen13/regsensitivity/issues/new?template=usage_report.md)
helps decide what comes next.
